## Which engine fits each workload? {#part-engines}

A recap of L11: the rides history in the lakehouse, read by different engines.

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each workload, choose the engine that fits it best. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Analysts occasionally ask new questions about trip history data, without idle billing :: Athena
  > Athena bills per TB of Data scanned and no query charge between queries (S3 storage is billed either way), which suits questions that come and go.
- Nightly job rewrites yesterday's trips data into a sorted Iceberg table; it runs about 10 minutes :: Glue job
  > A Glue job bills DPU-hours for the run only, so a regular batch pays for its 10 minutes and nothing else.
- Dashboard executes the same 20 large-scan queries every few minutes, all day :: Trino on EMR
  > Calculate the crossover first: at this load the cluster, billed per node-hour, costs less than paying per query (the review page works the numbers).
- :: Lambda
  > With custom layers and the maximum memory setting you might be able to run some of these workloads in Lambda, but it is not the best solution for any of them.
```

## Which store fits each workload? {#part-stores}

Operational and analytical stores side by side: DynamoDB, a relational database, S3 and the lakehouse.

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Match each workload to the store that fits it best. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- A game keeps each player's score as one small record, updated by player id tens of thousands of times a second at peak. Nothing joins it to other data :: DynamoDB
  > Small items, always found by one key, at a rate that changes with the game: what DynamoDB is built for.
- A shopping site reads and writes each visitor's cart by cart id on every page view, with ten times the traffic on sale days. No query joins carts :: DynamoDB
  > One key per request and traffic that jumps: DynamoDB scales on demand and answers in milliseconds.
- An order system runs one query that joins customers, orders and products :: Relational database (RDS)
  > Joins across tables are what a relational database does. DynamoDB has no joins.
- A video site stores each uploaded video, files of several gigabytes :: S3
  > A DynamoDB item is at most 400 KB. Large files go to S3, as objects.
- Analysts ask a new SQL question every week over 5 TB of order history from three years :: Lakehouse (Athena on Iceberg)
  > Ad hoc questions that scan a lot of history: columns in Parquet, billed by Data scanned.
- A nightly report adds up about 3 TB of sales records by product :: Lakehouse (Athena on Iceberg)
  > A scan of terabytes on DynamoDB would read every item, for hours and dollars. The lakehouse reads only the columns the report needs.
```

## Which reads need a strong read? {#part-reads}

Reads in the trip app: when a read may be a moment old, and when it must return the latest write.

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each read in the trip app, choose the least expensive option that meets its need. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- The driver app reads trip t-0042 back right after its own accept succeeded, to show the assigned driver :: Strongly consistent read
  > Read-after-write: an eventual read might come from a replica without the accept and show the trip still "requested".
- The driver app shows whether the passenger has cancelled, right after the passenger phoned the driver to say so :: Strongly consistent read
  > Another user's write the driver already knows about: an eventual read could still show the trip as active.
- The passenger app refreshes the driver's position on the map every two seconds, where an old position is acceptable :: Eventually consistent read
  > An old position is acceptable here, later refreshes replace it, and eventual reads cost half.
- The passenger app shows the fare right after the passenger's promo-code update succeeded :: Strongly consistent read
  > Read-after-write: the passenger just wrote, and an old fare on screen would look like the promo failed.
- A list of the passenger's past trips, where a trip that just finished may appear on the next refresh :: Eventually consistent read
  > An old list is acceptable on this screen, and eventual reads cost half.
- :: Federated query from Athena
  > A query taking seconds through a connector serves reports, not a screen that must open in milliseconds.
```

## Which problem is each situation? {#part-problems}

A food-delivery app keeps live orders in DynamoDB and order history in a lakehouse.

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Food-delivery app keeps orders in DynamoDB and order history in a lakehouse. Match each situation to the problem it shows. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- A customer edits the delivery address, and the confirmation screen right after shows the old one :: Replication lag
  > The read came from a replica that did not have the write yet. A strongly consistent read would have shown it.
- Two couriers both mark the same order "picked up", and the order ends up with the second courier's name :: Lost update
  > Both read "waiting" correctly. The second write replaced the first. A conditional write would have refused one.
- A nightly load into the lakehouse runs twice after a timeout, and yesterday's orders appear twice :: Non-idempotent load
  > Duplicates do not go away by waiting. An idempotent load (a `MERGE` keyed by order id over deduplicated input) would have left one copy.
- The link between two Regions fails, and the app in one Region returns errors for order updates until it returns :: Netsplit
  > The Region chose to refuse writes rather than let the two Regions disagree.
- :: Scan
  > A Scan is a specific way to read data, not one of these problems.
```
